result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.union()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the union of this graph with another graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L15551-L15634){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.union(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Union](/assets/graphs/union.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="G has edges A–B and B–D, which H shares, plus A–C (only in G, accent). H adds C–D (only in H, teal). The union keeps all four nodes and all four edges, each in the color of the graph it came from." width="100%"} Returns a new graph containing all nodes and edges from both graphs. Nodes with the same ID are merged, whatever their labels; where both graphs give the same node (or edge) a label, attribute, or weight, this graph's value takes precedence and the other graph fills in the rest. Duplicate edges are not added. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The graph to union with. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph containing all nodes and edges from both graphs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graphs have different directedness (one directed, one undirected). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Union takes the pointwise superset of nodes and edges, merging any nodes that share an ID; where attributes clash, the calling graph wins. Both operands must agree on directedness, because there is no principled way to fold a directed edge into an undirected graph without losing information. If either operand is weighted, so is the result. Use `disjoint_union()` when you want to keep node IDs strictly separate. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Nodes are matched by **ID**, not by label. Here both graphs number their nodes 1, 2, 3; `g2` adds an edge between nodes 2 and 3 that `g1` lacks, so the union has all three nodes and both edges: ::: {#952c1bee .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) g1.add_node(label="A") g1.add_node(label="B") g1.add_node(label="C") g1.add_edge("A", "B") g2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) g2.add_node(label="A") g2.add_node(label="B") g2.add_node(label="C") g2.add_edge("B", "C") result = g1.union(g2) result.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#27a9b888 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} result.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: This makes union a natural way to combine two snapshots of the same network taken at different times, folding in whatever new nodes or edges appeared: ::: {#32b0f159 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} t1 = ec.Graph(directed=False) t1.add_path_graph(3) # 1-2-3 t2 = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(1, 4): t2.add_node() t2.add_edge(1, 3) # a new direct connection combined = t1.union(t2) combined.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 3 ``` ::: :::
